research_questions: Could a bacterial-cellulose/SCOBY-like sheet have been used as a sorptive wrapping to take up oils from an embalmed body?
What would remain archaeologically after long-term degradation of a SCOBY pellicle?
Can oil be obtained from SCOBY itself, or only recovered after the material has absorbed external oil?

known_mummy_wrapping_material.finding: Microscopy, SEM and fibre-orientation studies identify sampled Egyptian mummy wrappings as flax/linen bast-fibre textiles with characteristic nodes, dislocations, fibre bundles and woven structure.

known_oil_relation.finding: Organic residue analyses repeatedly detect plant oil and/or animal fat, resins, waxes and related embalming mixtures impregnating linen wrappings.
known_oil_relation.interpretation: Published archaeological interpretation is application of preservative/odoriferous/hydrophobic embalming mixtures to bodies and wrappings, not extraction of endogenous body oil by the wrappings.

early_evidence.finding: Predynastic/Badarian funerary linen already preserves complex fat/oil/resin mixtures, showing that oil-bearing wrappings are much older than the mature Pharaonic embalming canon.

native_bacterial_cellulose.property: Native bacterial cellulose is strongly hydrophilic and water-retentive.
native_bacterial_cellulose.implication: A wet/raw SCOBY pellicle should not automatically be treated as a selective oil sorbent.

engineered_oil_sorbents.finding: Hydrophobically modified or aerogel-form bacterial-cellulose materials can absorb substantial quantities of oil; published examples include about 48.2 g/g for a stearic-acid-modified BC aerogel and 132-274 g/g for a carbonized BC aerogel.
engineered_oil_sorbents.boundary: These values belong to engineered modern materials and cannot be projected onto untreated ancient SCOBY-like pellicles.

can_oil_be_obtained_from_scoby.short_answer: Not as a meaningful intrinsic oil crop. SCOBY pellicle is primarily a cellulose-rich biofilm, not an oil-rich tissue.

intrinsic_fraction.interpretation: Trace or minor lipids may be chemically extractable from biomass, but this is different from obtaining a practical bulk oil comparable with seed, fruit or animal fat.

external_oil_recovery.route: If a SCOBY-derived cellulose material first absorbs external oil, that absorbed oil can in principle be recovered by an appropriate separation method.
external_oil_recovery.boundary: Recovery performance depends strongly on porosity, wettability, drying state and surface modification.

decay_fingerprint_gate.core_problem: Bacterial cellulose and plant cellulose share the same beta-1,4-glucan chemical backbone, so generic cellulose chemistry alone is not a unique ancient SCOBY fingerprint.
what_may_survive: microfibrillar/nanofibrillar morphology if preservation is exceptional
absorbed oils, fats, resins or waxes and their oxidation products
possibly residual biomolecular traces from embedded microbes, subject to severe preservation and contamination limits
what_is_likely_to_be_lost_or_ambiguous: most soluble sugars and organic acids
a unique chemical distinction from other purified cellulose after extensive degradation
best_discriminators_against_flax_or_papy: absence of flax bast-fibre nodes/dislocations and characteristic fibre cross-sections
presence of a continuous non-woven nanofibrillar cellulose mat
material chemistry unusually poor in plant-cell-wall accessory polymers while still cellulose-rich
independent microbial or fermentation-associated biomolecular evidence if preserved
decay_fingerprint_gate.archaeological_verdict: A degraded SCOBY-like material would be difficult to prove from chemistry alone; morphology plus context plus biomolecular evidence would be required.

mummy_oil_extraction_hypothesis.proposal: SCOBY-like cellulose sheets might hypothetically have functioned as sacrificial sorbent wraps that took up oily material from a body and were then removed for oil recovery.
current_counterevidence: studied mummy wrappings are overwhelmingly linen/flax textiles rather than non-woven bacterial-cellulose sheets
embalming residues indicate deliberate addition of oils/fats/resins to wrappings
known embalming instructions and residue studies support preservation/treatment functions rather than oil harvesting

safe_modern_test_gate.purpose: Test only the material mechanism without human remains.
samples: hydrophobized SCOBY-derived sheet if separately validated
linen control of equal area and dry mass
test_liquids: water/oil mixture as a separate selectivity test
measurements: oil recovery fraction after standardized mechanical pressing
repeatability across at least three independent samples
safe_modern_test_gate.decision_rule: Only if an unmodified or historically plausible cellulose sheet shows reproducible oil uptake and recoverability should the archaeological sorbent hypothesis remain experimentally interesting.

search_targets_for_egyptology: non-woven cellulose-like sheets in mummy contexts
amorphous cellulose-rich layers between body and linen
instructions involving temporary wrapping followed by removal, squeezing or recovery of liquid
vessels or tools associated with wringing/pressing used immediately after body wrapping
GC-MS residues where oil is localized in an anomalous sacrificial sheet rather than ordinary linen
